records.name: Washington
records.current_summary:
A July 2026 national legal-risk map lists Washington among the federation's fifteen Most Protective states, naming it specifically for comprehensive health-insurance requirements covering gender-affirming procedures — including facial-hair removal and an expanded range of treatments — and for refuge protections for people fleeing restrictive states. Equality-map research (data as of 25 September 2026) counts Washington among the healthcare "shield"-law states that protect recipients and providers from out-of-state civil or criminal action.

Federal 2025 document and passport restrictions still apply here as across the federation.
records.current_localsOnly: The comprehensive insurance-coverage mandate the July 2026 map names Washington for is a resident-facing detail; it shapes care access, not a visitor's exposure.

sources.claim: July 2026 assessment: Washington named among the 'Most Protective' states AND among states (with Colorado, Hawaii, Maryland) with comprehensive health-insurance laws covering facial hair removal and an expanded range of gender-affirming procedures, plus refugee protections for people fleeing hostile states; two November ballot initiatives (I-001, I-638) are flagged as targeting transgender residents.

records.name: Isole
records.current_summary:
At roughly 5 a.m. on 26 April 2025 three young men were beaten in a fast-food restaurant in this region's largest city solely because they were gay; the victims were hospitalised, video of the attack later circulated publicly, and the prosecutor's office reconstructed the sequence - insults and threats first, then the physical assault.

A June 2026 press survey of reporting from the island documents a sustained pattern rather than isolated events: rising homophobic bullying, violence against LGBTIA+ people and associated suicides, with multiple cases listed. The pattern is qualitative but official: a hospitalisation-level public assault and an prosecutorial reconstruction sit alongside a growing documented toll.

sources.claim: TG LA7: 26 April 2025, a fast-food restaurant in Catania — three young men beaten because they were gay; the prosecutor's office (Procura etnea) reconstructed the sequence of insults and threats before the physical assault, and video of the attack circulated publicly.

Catania-based outlet (5 June 2026): 'Omofobia in Sicilia, continuano le violenze' — a 2026 follow-up cataloguing continuing assaults and suicide cases across Sicilian towns, the record's evidence that the 2025 pattern has not stopped.

records.name: Alberta
records.current_summary:
In December 2024 this province enacted a package of three laws affecting transgender people as a class: school rules requiring parental notification and consent before staff use a student's gender-related chosen name or pronouns; a prohibition on puberty blockers and hormone therapy for minors; and related vital-statistics amendments. Trans and intersex advocacy organisations said at the time they would continue legal action.

In December 2025 the government invoked the constitutional override clause to shield all three laws from judicial remedy. Two national 2SLGBTQ+ organisations, together with five gender-diverse young people, say the constitutional challenge continues despite the shield - a provincial posture of legislating trans-targeting rules and then placing them beyond the courts.
records.current_localsOnly: The school pronoun/opt-in rules, the minors' care ban and the vital-statistics amendment bind residents' institutions — a visitor uses their home passport and never touches them; their traveller-facing weight is the climate signal and the street pattern, not the letter of the laws.
records.current_outOfScope: Alberta's second-highest provincial 2021 gender-related homicide rate of women and girls (0.68 per 100,000) is a general gendered-violence base-rate proxy, not a trans-specific measure; it should not move a trans-traveller rating.

sources.claim: CBC (4 Dec 2024): Alberta's trio of trans-youth bills passed final legislative stage — the Education Amendment Act 2024 (parental opt-in for classroom instruction, student pronoun and sport rules), a health-statutes act barring certain gender-affirming care for minors, plus sports policy. Egale Canada and the Skipping Stone Foundation announced constitutional litigation, calling the package discriminatory.

CBC (Dec 2024): Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, passed at the tail of the fall sitting, invoking the Charter's notwithstanding clause to shield the three trans-youth laws from legal challenge for years; Egale Canada, Skipping Stone Foundation and five families said their court challenge to Bill 26 continues regardless. Result: laws in force, constitutional litigation pending.

records.name: Saskatchewan
records.current_summary:
In August 2023 the provincial government announced school policies requiring parents to be asked for permission before staff use a student's preferred name or pronouns (for pupils under 16), parents to be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and third-party school programs to be paused. The province's senior trial court struck the rule down as unconstitutional; the government responded by legislating the consent rule into the Education Act and invoking the notwithstanding clause to immunise it from judicial review.

The matter went to the province's Court of Appeal, which largely allowed the government's appeal in August 2025; a current-status verification found no later ruling, leaving the re-legislated, shielded policy standing. For a visitor the education rule is primarily resident-facing; the durable signal is institutional: a provincial government re-legislating a policy a court had voided and shielding that from rights review - official hostility hardened past ordinary litigation.
records.current_localsOnly: The under-16 parental-consent name/pronoun rule, its legislated form (Education Act s.197.4) and the court proceedings around it are school-policy matters facing resident students; visitors encounter them only as a signal of provincial posture toward trans people.
records.current_outOfScope: The 2021 gender-related homicide rate (1.03 per 100k, the highest provincial figure cited) is a non-trans-specific proxy covering women and girls generally and should not be read as traveler-facing trans risk.

sources.claim: Government of Saskatchewan education-ministry news release (22 Aug 2023) announcing the parental inclusion and consent policies: schools must seek parent/guardian permission before changing the preferred name and pronouns of students under 16, parents must be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and third-party school programs were paused. The release that started the court challenge.

Saskatchewan (Minister of Education) v UR Pride Centre, 2025 SKCA 74 (11 Aug 2025): the Court of Appeal set aside the 2023 chambers decision — courts lack jurisdiction to test s.1/s.15 Charter breaches of the school pronoun-notice policy where s.33 was invoked — so the policy stands. Supersedes the injunction-era chambers ruling.

sources.title: Saskatchewan Appeal Court says challenge of province's pronoun law can continue
sources.claim: The Saskatchewan Court of Appeal ruled Aug. 11, 2025 on the provincial government's appeal in the challenge to the school pronoun law, granting the government's appeal in part but holding that a judge has jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits Charter rights, and that (LGBTQ+ group) UR Pride's litigation may continue in the Court of King's Bench. The 2023 law requires parental consent before children under 16 change their names or pronouns at school, and the government had argued its use of the notwithstanding clause should end the challenge entirely. Egale Canada co-counsel Bennett Jensen said UR Pride will continue the litigation, noting students had been 'living under the reality of this law' for two years. This mainstream coverage independently traces the record's claim that the appeal court largely allowed the government's appeal while keeping the merits challenge alive.

sources.title: Amnesty International Canada welcomes ruling in court challenge to Saskatchewan pronoun law
sources.claim: Amnesty International Canada welcomed the Aug. 11, 2025 decision of the Court of Appeal for Saskatchewan as a 'meaningful victory for the protection of human rights in Canada', saying courts can still determine whether the province's anti-trans pronoun law violates the Charter and issue a declaration to that effect even where the notwithstanding clause shields the law from being struck down. Amnesty participated as an intervenor in the appeal, arguing that use of the clause must align with Canada's international-law obligation to provide an effective remedy. The piece corroborates the durable signal this record draws from the case: a consent and name-change rule for transgender pupils shielded from ordinary rights review while litigation continues.

sources.title: Supreme Court to weigh in on Saskatchewan's school pronoun case
sources.claim: On Nov. 6, 2025 the Supreme Court of Canada said it will hear the appeals in the challenge to Saskatchewan's school pronoun law, which since 2023 has required parental consent before children under 16 change their names or pronouns at school and has been shielded by the province's invocation of the Charter's notwithstanding clause (a five-year override). Both the province and LGBTQ+ group UR Pride appealed the Court of Appeal decision that the challenge can continue, and asked for the hearing to be expedited alongside the challenge to Quebec's Bill 21. The grant is the key later development for this record: no merits ruling has changed the policy, but the constitutionality of the re-legislated, shielded consent rule is now before Canada's highest court.

freshness_all.fact: Policy remains in force: 2025 SKCA 74 allowed the government appeal in part; courts lack jurisdiction to void it while the notwithstanding clause stands

records.name: Scotland
records.current_summary:
This region's prosecution system names anti-trans crime as its own charging category: the region's 2021 hate-crime statute created a dedicated transgender-identity aggravation, and the prosecuting authority reported 104 charges carrying it in 2025-26 (up 21% on 86 the year before), while police recorded 8,538 hate crimes in the provision's first full year. For a visitor who is assaulted or harassed, the machinery exists to see the offence counted and charged by name.

The region's parliament also passed a more expansive self-declaration gender-recognition law with a two-thirds majority in December 2022 - evidence of markedly more trans-accepting regional institutions - only for the central government to block it with the first-ever use of a statutory veto order; verification as of September 2026 confirms the bill fell and remains not law, with no revival. The same UK-wide rules on legal sex and single-sex services apply here as across the union state.
records.current_localsOnly: The blocked Gender Recognition Reform Bill concerns self-declaration birth-certificate procedures for residents; the voided prison guidance determines placement of those in Scottish custody, which residents and any detained visitor share.

sources.claim: COPFS 'Hate crime in Scotland, 2025-26' (30 Jun 2026): 7,115 hate-crime charges total, up 17% on 2024-25 and the highest since 2003-04; sexual-orientation aggravation 2,062 charges (second commonest category); transgender-identity aggravation 104 charges, up 21% from 86 — the highest since the 2021 Act took effect.

Scottish Government 'Hate crimes recorded by the police in Scotland, 2024-25' (pub. 17 Feb 2026): police recorded 8,538 hate crimes, with the highest rates per 10,000 residents in Glasgow City and City of Edinburgh (about 32.25 each); 62% carried a race aggravator and just over a quarter a sexual-orientation aggravator — first annual report under the Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021.

records.name: Distrito Federal
records.current_summary:
CDMX recorded the highest transfeminicide toll in the country in 2024 — 17 LGBT+ homicides, of which 11 were trans women — and remains among the highest-count states in 2025. The raw violence data is a negative signal for a visitor, though part of the elevated count reflects the city's superior reporting infrastructure rather than proportionally higher danger.

Counterbalanced by the strongest institutional response of any Mexican state: transfeminicide made a distinct crime in July 2024 ("Ley Paola Buenrostro", the second state to do so); a dedicated Transfeminicide Investigation Unit created December 2024 covering all violent deaths of trans women; a prosecutor's protocol (Acuerdo FGJCDMX/04/2025) requiring feminist-context investigation with immediate-action deadlines (72h/48h); a new Gender Police launched August 2025 with 30 patrol units. Long-standing LGR since 2014, extended to 12-year-olds by 2021 decree. For a visitor assaulted in CDMX, there is trained machinery to investigate; in Nuevo León (0.40) or Michoacán (0.40) there is none.

Modestly above the national 0.55: the protective and investigative framework is the strongest in Mexico and materially changes what a visitor who encounters violence or discrimination faces after the fact, even though the pre-violence risk data is the country's worst.
records.current_localsOnly: The capital's administrative LGR regime — in force since 2014 and opened to 12-year-olds by 2021 decree — is a resident-facing civil-registry procedure; visitors never enter it.

sources.claim: Annual report (May 2025) by a Mexican LGBT+ news collective on homicides of LGBT+ people in Mexico in 2024: for the first time CDMX topped the national count with 17 homicides, 11 of them trans women, ahead of Nuevo León (5); 115 recorded violent incidents nationally, of which 59 killings. The primary state-by-state violence data.

NOTE: cached page returned only site navigation; the underlying CNN en Español report (19 July 2024) covers Mexico City's congress approving transfeminicide as a distinct crime in the penal code — the reform dubbed the "Ley Paola Buenrostro" after a trans woman murdered in 2016, making CDMX the second state to create the offence.

Proceso (20 Dec 2024): CDMX created a dedicated Transfeminicide Investigation Unit; its investigators may no longer demand legal name/gender change or medical documentation from trans people. Context: on 18 Jul 2024 CDMX became the country's second entity to typify transfeminicidio, after the local congress passed the 'Paola Buenrostro' law (named for a trans woman murdered in 2016).

CDMX instrument FGJCDMX/04/2025: article 148-Ter was added to the local code on 23 Aug 2024 typifying transfeminicidio — killing of a trans woman or feminine-spectrum person by reason of gender identity or expression — and the agreement sets initial-response protocol rules for such cases alongside feminicide investigations.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (404); the underlying Proceso report (25 Aug 2025) covers the mayor of Mexico City launching the new Gender Police with 30 patrol units to handle cases of violence against women and girls in the capital.

freshness_all.fact: CDMX remains Mexico's most protective jurisdiction: gender-ID change since 2008, conversion-therapy ban 2020, non-binary registration added 2025; the 2024 transfeminicide aggravated-offence reform stands.

records.who: MEX/Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave
records.name: Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave
records.current_summary:
Veracruz led the national LGBT+ fatality count for four consecutive years — in 2021 alone, 10 recorded violent deaths of LGBT+ people, ahead of Guanajuato (9), Estado de México (7) and Chihuahua (6), with 19 of 32 states recording victims that year. In 2025 the state closed the year with at least 15 hate crimes against the LGBT+ community; a January 2025 running total put 460 hate-crime cases unresolved, and Emblematic cases have arrests but no final sentences. Activists cite 'rezago y archivamiento de expedientes' (deliberate filing-away of cases), and the state prosecutor's office has lost investigative files entirely; in one emblematic case (a chef killed in February 2021) the family reported that the homicide file had simply disappeared, and organisers call the 2025 pride march a platform against that impunity. The killing of 'Luis M', a 27-year-old trans woman stabbed to death in a motel in Oluta on 19 November 2025, came after the state observatory had already counted 9 hate crimes earlier that year, three of them against trans women; the Coatzacoalcos-Oluta corridor is named in the national notes as Veracruz's concentration zone. The danger inside the state is metro-and-corridor concentrated rather than uniform.

The only institutional counterweight is recent: Veracruz passed its gender-identity civil-code reform in 2025 with no age limit, among the last to legislate one (2025): 22 of 32 states had a procedure by March 2025. Before that, a visitor or resident had no legal route to correct documents. The absence of any functioning investigation or prosecution machinery — distinct from other states where laws exist but enforcement is weak — makes the impunity here total.

Context for comparison: Guanajuato, which carries sustained violence too, has a comprehensive diversity law and a court-forced recognition procedure; Nayarit typified the transfeminicide offence first in the country (March 2024). Veracruz's four-year lethality record combined with explicit case-archiving and lost files represents the worst enforcement climate, and its legal framework arrived latest and is least functional.
records.current_outOfScope: General insecurity in the north of the state (municipalities with most internally displaced people from armed-group violence) affects all travellers; it matters here only insofar as it further disables the reporting and investigation channel for anti-LGBT violence.

sources.claim: Letra S 'Muertes violentas de personas LGBT+ en México — Informe 2021' (May 2022): Veracruz led the national count of violent deaths of LGBT+ people for the fourth consecutive year, with 10 recorded cases in 2021, followed by Guanajuato (9), Estado de México (7) and Chihuahua (6); 19 of 32 states recorded victims. The report notes under-reporting: in a third of 2021 cases no name was published, and in 43 percent the sex recorded was male without attention to gender identity.
Diario de Xalapa (headline; body not extractable from cache): Veracruz closed 2025 with 15 recorded hate crimes against the LGBT community.

Jornada Veracruz: state prosecutor holds several open LGBT-murder files per activist Leonardo Ruiz (Orgullo Xalapa), including Edhibaldo Presa Parra, a Universidad Veracruzana professor found dead on 7 Jan; activists say hate-crime suspicion rests on motive patterns (avenaia, aggravants and the victim's orientation) and blame impunity in the FGE, while 'Soy Humano' data put 2024 below the national average.

LetraS Excela annual impunity report (7 May 2026): of 60 LGBT+ people murdered nationwide in 2025, 35 (58.3%) were trans women — a national trans-women homicide rate of 23.7 per 100,000. State ranking: Puebla 7, then Veracruz and Guanajuato 6 each; includes a Veracruz case (Oluta motel killing, Nov 2025).
